text: So the king and Haman came to feast with Queen Esther.

versions.text: So the king and Haman came to dine with Queen Esther.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb is "to drink," tying this verse to the repeated "banquet of wine" motif in the chapter (vv. 2, 7, 8). "Dine" shifts the image to eating; "feast" (or "drink") preserves the link with the wine banquet mentioned in the following verses.

text: And again on this second day, as they drank their wine, the king said to Esther, "What is your petition, Queen Esther? It shall be granted you. What is your request? Up to half the kingdom, and it shall be done."
Queen Esther answered, "If I have found favor in your eyes, O king, and if it pleases the king, let my life be granted me as my petition, and my people as my request.

For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, killed, and annihilated. If we had merely been sold as slaves and servant girls, I would have kept silent, for such trouble would not be worth disturbing the king."
Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, "Who is he? Where is the man who has dared to do such a thing?"
Esther said, "The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman!" And Haman stood terrified before the king and queen.

In his fury the king rose from the wine banquet and went out into the palace garden, while Haman stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he saw that the king had already determined his ruin.

versions.text: The king rose from the wine in his fury and went out into the palace garden, while Haman stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he saw that the king had already determined his ruin.
versions.explanation: "Rose from the wine" is slightly clipped; the Hebrew is "the banquet of wine," the same phrase rendered elsewhere in the chapter. Fronting "in his fury" also gives a smoother spoken rhythm and avoids the momentary ambiguity of "rose from the wine in his fury."

text: When the king returned from the palace garden to the banquet hall, Haman had thrown himself on the couch where Esther was reclining. The king exclaimed, "Will he even assault the queen while she is with me in my own house?" As the words left the king's mouth, they covered Haman's face.

Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs attending the king, said, "Look, the gallows Haman made for Mordecai, who spoke up for the king's good, is standing at Haman's house, fifty cubits high."[fn] The king said, "Hang him on it."

versions.text: Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs attending the king, said, "Look, the gallows Haman made for Mordecai, whose word saved the king, is standing at Haman's house, fifty cubits high." The king said, "Hang him on it."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew says Mordecai "spoke good concerning/on behalf of the king," that is, he reported the plot. "Whose word saved the king" adds an interpretive claim (salvation) not present in the text; a closer rendering keeps the sense of speaking on the king's behalf while remaining readable aloud.

versions.text: Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs attending the king, said, "Look, the gallows Haman made for Mordecai, who spoke up for the king's good, is standing at Haman's house, fifty cubits high." The king said, "Hang him on it."
versions.explanation: Consider a footnote giving the modern equivalent of fifty cubits (about 23 meters / 75 feet), and noting that the Hebrew word for gallows is literally "tree" or "wooden pole." This helps hearers grasp the scale without interrupting the read-aloud flow.

text: So they hanged Haman on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai, and the king's fury subsided.
